newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Differences cloud planned Tajik peace deal.
newsitem.headline: Differences cloud planned Tajik peace deal.

text.p: A stalled prisoner exchange and haggling over power-sharing threaten to scupper an accord to end civil war in Tajikistan, a member of the country's Islamic opposition was quoted as saying on Thursday.

Akbar Turajonzoda, the opposition's deputy leader, was cited by the Russian news agency Interfax as saying his faction would not sign a peace agreement on Friday in Moscow if the two issues were not cleared up.

"Representatives from both sides are holding consultations at this moment on these questions but the absence of (Tajik) President (Imomali) Rakhmonov at the talks is hampering a mutually acceptable decision," Turajonzoda told Interfax in Moscow.

But the agency, citing Tajik government sources, later reported that Rakhmonov might meet with opposition leader Sayid Abdullo Nuri late on Thursday if the two delegations fail to reach agreement on the issues.
Rakhmonov arrived in Moscow on Thursday morning for final talks before Friday's planned signing, to take place in the Kremlin and to be witnessed by Russian President Boris Yeltsin.
Earlier this week, Turajonzoda threatened to boycott the signing, citing the same issues.
But diplomats say he is hardline and other senior opposition officials said this week they intended to sign the agreement on Friday.
On Thursday, Mizrob Kabirov, Rakhmonov's security adviser, told Interfax that the government was "ready even today" to start an exchange of prisoners.

Tajik officials and observers say the planned accord is the first real chance of ending the war in the former Soviet republic bordering Afghanistan and China. Four years of fighting claimed tens of thousands of lives and made many more homeless.
A ceasefire -- brokered by Iran, Russia and the United Nations -- has held for an unprecedented seven months. Earlier agreements often collapsed as soon as they were signed.
"In four years, this is the first real window onto the peace we've been waiting for," said a Tajik government official, on condition of anonymity.
The accord envisages the creation of a 26-member National Commission for Reconciliation, to be chaired by Nuri, with places to be divided equally between each side.
Rakhmonov, who survived an assassination attempt in April, remains president but 30 percent of government posts must be given over to the opposition.
Elections for a new parliament must take place before the end of 1998. Opposition guerrillas must integrate with government forces or lay down their weapons.
But a slew of troubles cloud the guarded optimism surrounding the deal.
The inhabitants of Dushanbe are apprehensive about the return of 460 armed opposition guerrillas to the city and fear their presence could spark more fighting.

Each camp contains hardliners who have little trust for their opponents while the power-sharing arrangement has sidelined a bewildering array of armed groups and local chieftains in the republic of 5.7 million.
With the economy in tatters, government and opposition face the immediate problem of how to deal with armed criminal bands which operate with virtual impunity throughout the republic.
